title: What does Minnesota's AWAIR program require, and how does training fit in?
description: Minn. Stat. 182.653 subd. 8 (AWAIR): who needs a written program, its five elements, annual review, safety committees and training, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: Minnesota Statutes section 182.653, subdivision 8, requires employers in industries listed in Minnesota Rules part 5208.1500 to keep a written workplace accident and injury reduction (AWAIR) program with five elements, including how the program is communicated to employees so they know their hazards and controls, and to review it at least annually. AWAIR does not set a course or hours; training is the main way employers meet the communication element.
keyTakeaways: AWAIR applies only to employers in the North American Industry Classification codes listed in Minnesota Rules part 5208.1500, which cover industries such as crop farming, utilities and construction.
The written program must describe five things: responsibilities, hazard identification and control, communication to employees, accident investigation, and enforcement of safe work rules.
Employers must conduct and document a review of the program at least annually and document how its procedures are being met.
Employers of more than 25 employees, and smaller employers covered by AWAIR, must also run a safety committee under section 182.676.
Separate statutory training, such as Employee Right-to-Know training on hazardous substances, applies before initial assignment and at intervals of no more than one year.
regulator: Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry, Minnesota Occupational Safety and Health Administration (MNOSHA)
appliesTo: Employers in the North American Industry Classification codes listed in Minnesota Rules part 5208.1500
Managers, supervisors and employees whose responsibilities the written program must describe
All affected employees, who must be informed of work-related hazards and controls

sections.heading: What is the Minnesota AWAIR program?

blocks.text: AWAIR is Minnesota's required written safety and health program for higher-risk industries. Minnesota Statutes section 182.653, subdivision 8, states that a covered employer "must establish a written work place accident and injury reduction program that promotes safe and healthful working conditions and is based on clearly stated goals and objectives for meeting those goals." The Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry, through Minnesota OSHA, enforces it.

According to the Department's AWAIR page, Minnesota adopted the requirement on January 1, 1991, and in 2005 the Legislature amended the statute to allow North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes to define the covered list. The Department published an updated AWAIR guidance booklet in June 2026. This page states the position as at November 2026.

AWAIR resembles California's Injury and Illness Prevention Program and Washington's accident prevention program in purpose, but it is narrower in scope and less detailed about training. Compare [Cal/OSHA IIPP training requirements](/regulations/cal-osha-iipp-training-requirements) and [Washington accident prevention program training](/regulations/washington-accident-prevention-program-training).

sections.heading: Which Minnesota employers must have an AWAIR program?

blocks.text: Only employers in the industry classifications listed in Minnesota Rules part 5208.1500. That rule states that employers in the listed NAICS classifications "must comply with Minnesota Statutes, section 182.653, subdivision 8," using the 2022 edition of NAICS. The list includes, for example, crop farming codes from 111110 soybean farming onward, utilities such as electric power generation and natural gas distribution, and construction codes including roofing, framing and electrical contractors.

Under subdivision 9, the commissioner must justify each listed industry by its safety or workers' compensation record, an employer must comply six months after its classification is placed on the list, and the list must be updated every five years. The current rule text was published electronically on March 28, 2025.

blocks.title: Check the rule, not a summary
blocks.text: As at November 2026, the Department's AWAIR web page still describes the list as using the 2012 NAICS edition, while Minnesota Rules part 5208.1500 itself refers to the 2022 edition. Use the rule text on the Revisor of Statutes site to confirm whether your code is listed.

sections.heading: What must the written AWAIR program describe?

blocks.text: Five elements, each of which has a training dimension. The table maps the statutory elements to the people they apply to, how often they recur, and the evidence a Minnesota OSHA investigator would expect.

blocks.text: Subdivision 8(b) adds that the employer "must conduct and document a review of the work place accident and injury reduction program at least annually and document how procedures set forth in the program are met." Training records are the most direct way to show that element (3) is being met.

Not by name. The statute requires the program to describe how it will be communicated so employees "are informed of work-related hazards and controls," but it sets no course, hours or interval. Subdivision 10 limits the commissioner's rulemaking for AWAIR to the industry list, so there are no detailed AWAIR training rules.

The Department's June 2026 AWAIR booklet treats training as the main communication method. It says safety training "should go beyond the minimum required by OSHA regulations, such as hazard communication and employee right-to-know," that supervisors "should receive at least as much safety and health training as their employees, if not more," that training content "must cover emergency procedures as well as normal day-to-day activities," and that there should be some method to assess understanding, such as written tests and quizzes, trainee demonstrations and on-the-job observation. It also identifies the start of a new job assignment and material, process or procedural changes as critical times for communication.

These are guidance, not statutory duties, but an investigator reviewing whether a program is effective is likely to look for them. See [how to design competency assessments](/guides/how-to-design-competency-assessments).

sections.heading: What other Minnesota training duties sit alongside AWAIR?

blocks.text: The same section, 182.653, contains specific training duties that apply whether or not the employer is on the AWAIR list. Subdivision 4b, Employee Right-to-Know, requires hazardous substance training before an employee's initial assignment to a workplace where they may be routinely exposed, additional instruction when new substances are introduced, and updates "at intervals no greater than one year." Subdivision 4c applies the same structure to harmful physical agents, and subdivision 4d covers waste disposal training for certain waste service employers.

Section 182.676 requires every public or private employer of more than 25 employees to run a joint labor-management safety committee, and employers of 25 or fewer to run one if they are covered by AWAIR. Committees must hold regularly scheduled meetings, and employee members must be selected by employees. Failure to establish or administer a required committee can be cited as a serious violation.

In practice, an AWAIR program is the frame that lists these obligations by role. A [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) that shows Right-to-Know topics, equipment training and supervisor training against each job makes the annual review straightforward. See also [OSHA hazard communication training](/regulations/osha-hazard-communication-training-requirements) for the federal equivalent.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each AWAIR element to the hazards, controls and roles it covers, so the annual review can show which employees were informed of which hazards and when, alongside the Right-to-Know annual updates. See [operational procedures programs](/programs/operational-procedures).

faqs.q: How do I know if my Minnesota business needs an AWAIR program?
faqs.a: Check your North American Industry Classification code against Minnesota Rules part 5208.1500 on the Revisor of Statutes site. If your code is listed, section 182.653, subdivision 8 applies, with compliance due six months after a classification is added to the list.

faqs.q: How often must an AWAIR program be reviewed?
faqs.a: At least annually. Subdivision 8(b) requires the employer to conduct and document the review and to document how the procedures in the program are being met.

faqs.q: Is annual safety training required in Minnesota?
faqs.a: AWAIR does not set an annual training interval. Employee Right-to-Know training under section 182.653, subdivisions 4b and 4c, must be updated at intervals of no more than one year for employees routinely exposed to hazardous substances or harmful physical agents.

faqs.q: Do small AWAIR employers need a safety committee?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 182.676 requires employers of 25 or fewer employees to establish and administer a safety committee if they are subject to section 182.653, subdivision 8. Employers of more than 25 must have one regardless.
